key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit-card debt, because nudged users chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
methodology: Field experiment on live credit-card accounts tracking payment behavior over six months (Guttman-Kenney et al., NBER 2023).
why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's core worry: a nudge changed nominal enrollment behavior (23% fewer minimum-only payers) without moving the underlying financial outcome, and reduced autopay enrollment increased missed payments among liquidity-constrained users -- exactly the enrolment-without-engagement pattern support flagged.
limitations: Credit-card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
shrouding is a different manipulation than opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing
relevance_reason: Consumer financial nudge field experiment showing enrollment change without amount change and heterogeneous harm to liquidity-constrained users -- near-identical mechanism to the round-up decision.

key_finding: A state-of-the-art review concludes automatic enrollment and default investment options raise short-term participation but can suppress long-term participant engagement, an effect that varies with financial literacy.
methodology: Narrative literature review/overview of defined-contribution plan design research. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives a current synthesis of the persistence-vs-engagement trade-off, useful as background for what to expect from a default even though the underlying plans are employer-run.
limitations: Entirely employer-sponsored DC retirement plans, not a consumer app
no consolidated effect sizes given in abstract
relevance_reason: Broad recent overview of the adjacent employer-plan literature the brief says is relevant by analogy but not directly transferable.

key_finding: Default enrollment raises short-term retirement participation but induces behavioral inertia -- low contribution rates, non-management of accounts, and account churn -- undermining long-term welfare gains from enrollment alone.
methodology: Narrative policy analysis of U.S. default-enrollment retirement research. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: States plainly the support team's objection in policy terms: participation is not the same as welfare, and passive enrollees disengage -- argues for pairing any opt-out default with reminders/education rather than trusting the enrollment number.
limitations: U.S. employer retirement system, not a consumer banking app
narrative rather than systematic review
no quantitative effect sizes in abstract
relevance_reason: Directly argues the 'enrollment lift is vanity' position the brief asks us to evaluate, though in the employer-pension setting.

key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework showing that downstream effects of defaults depend on the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and that findings on persistence are currently inconsistent across studies.
methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing consumer-default literature into a taxonomy and research agenda. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the moderator variables (time course, prior preference strength, trade-off salience) that should shape what we measure at 6-12 months to know whether round-up enrollment is a durable behavior change or just inertia.
limitations: Theoretical/synthesis paper, not new empirical estimates
not specific to financial products
relevance_reason: Most direct general-consumer treatment of exactly the persistence/downstream-effects question the brief raises, independent of the employer-pension literature.

key_finding: Natural experiments in Medicare Part D show default assignment has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug use, and beneficiary passivity is largely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default plans among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the manipulation-risk scenario the brief worries about: a default can stick even when it actively harms the enrolled person, which is the strongest argument against blanket opt-out without safeguards.
limitations: Government-administered health-insurance default, not a self-directed consumer financial app
low-income Medicare population differs from the app's user base
relevance_reason: Best available evidence that default stickiness is insensitive to option value, informing the distributional/manipulation-risk question even though the domain is health insurance rather than savings.

key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults escalate on the first scheduled date.
methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans tracking enrollment, escalation, and withdrawal dynamics over years.
why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative rebuttal to 'defaults always help': the same erosion mechanisms -- disengagement, opt-out over time, and withdrawal of nominal balances -- apply directly to a liquid round-up pot, where switching/withdrawal costs are even lower than in a 401(k), so the true long-run lift from opt-out enrollment is likely smaller than the headline enrollment number suggests.
limitations: Employer 401(k) plans with vesting and job-turnover dynamics not present in a banking app
no consumer product engagement or complaint data
relevance_reason: The tracking-attrition methodology (measuring nominal enrollment/escalation against actual retained, active saving over time) is the direct method transfer for auditing whether round-up 'enrollment' numbers reflect real engagement.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment for low-income employees in Germany's public pension system raised participation by 23 percentage points, but most enrolled individuals actively opted back out, and the default effect was strongest among people unaware of their enrollment status.
methodology: Natural experiment using nationwide policy rollout, linking administrative and survey data.
why_it_matters: Shows that a large headline default effect (23pp) can coexist with majority opt-out and that the effect concentrates among the least-informed -- a distributional pattern the brief specifically wants surfaced before choosing opt-out.
limitations: Public pension auto-enrollment, not a consumer banking app
opt-out driven by unfamiliarity, which may not describe app users who see the feature at sign-up
relevance_reason: Recent, large default-effect estimate with an explicit awareness/heterogeneity finding relevant to who is helped versus who is nominally enrolled.

key_finding: Auto-enrollment's boost to retirement participation and contributions, robust at 12 months, is attenuated by 36 months, with modest average savings gains but a significant reduction in savings inequality; a life-cycle model estimates the effective switching cost at about $250, lower than earlier estimates.
methodology: Panel analysis of 100+ US retirement plans and a UK representative panel, combined with a structural life-cycle consumption-savings model.
why_it_matters: Provides a concrete medium-run (36-month) decay estimate for a default's effect size and shows the switching-cost framework used to interpret it -- a template for what to track at the round-up feature's 6-12 month mark and how small effective frictions can still explain large enrollment gaps.
limitations: Employer/pension retirement savings, illiquid relative to a round-up pot
switching-cost estimate calibrated to a structural model, not directly observed
relevance_reason: Best available medium-run persistence estimate and distributional (inequality-reduction) finding in the closest available literature.

key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person sample from five European countries, default nudges shift investment risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower clients' rating of the advisor's advice, especially when the default is one the client ends up refusing, with perceived honesty mediating the effect.
methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment, on default framing in investment/risk-taking decisions.
why_it_matters: Directly evidences the EU manipulation-risk trade-off named in the brief: even an effective default can damage perceived trustworthiness and be read as manipulative, which argues for active choice or individualized defaults over a one-size-fits-all opt-out multiplier, and cautions on how the pre-set level is framed.
limitations: Wealth-management/investment advice setting rather than a round-up savings toggle
advice-rating outcome, not actual retention or complaint data
relevance_reason: European, consumer-facing experimental evidence on when a default is perceived as helpful versus manipulative -- precisely the reputational-risk question the brief raises, and it touches the preset-level anchoring question too.

key_finding: With automatic 401(k) enrollment, participation exceeds 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accept both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and a conservative default fund, and half still do at three years -- participation gains and low-default anchoring roughly offset each other in overall asset accumulation, though the lower tail of savers benefits clearly.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking 401(k) participation, default acceptance, and asset accumulation over three years.
why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most participants for years, which is the single strongest piece of evidence for choosing the multiplier level carefully rather than defaulting to whatever is administratively convenient.
limitations: Employer 401(k) setting from an older era of retirement research, cited as the classic study the brief says to weight less heavily
no online/app context
relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-at-default-level result the current literature builds on and argues with; directly informs the multiplier pre-selection question even though dated and off-domain.

key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both frictions together), and adding a lower preset option (15%) to an existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer-welfare gain from full customization at only 5.4% revenue cost.
methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6M transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey of true preferences, with counterfactual simulation.
why_it_matters: Gives a transferable mechanism and welfare-tradeoff framework for exactly the multiplier-menu decision: it shows how adding one more preset level near what people actually want can recover most of the welfare gain of a blank field, without abandoning defaults -- directly informs whether to ship 1x/2x/5x or something denser, and shows opt-out friction (not just anchoring) drives adherence.
limitations: Tipping decisions on a single transaction, not a repeated savings enrollment choice
no engagement/withdrawal outcomes over time
relevance_reason: A consumer, self-directed, app-like default-menu setting with a rigorous mechanism and welfare analysis of preset-level design -- closest available evidence for the multiplier question.

key_finding: In a UK opt-in short-term savings account offered through employers, take-up was very low (no more than 0.7% of eligible employees), but among those who did opt in, 96% retained a balance and 87% received an automatic contribution at 12 months.
methodology: Field study of a payroll-deduction short-term (liquid) savings product introduced at five UK firms, tracking take-up and 12-month account activity.
why_it_matters: The closest available analogue to a liquid, withdrawable round-up pot: it shows opt-in alone yields excellent retention among enrollees but negligible overall reach, which is the strongest argument in the file for not relying on opt-in if broad enrollment is a goal, and supports testing opt-out or active choice instead.
limitations: Delivered through an employer payroll system, so the trusted-intermediary effect the brief says doesn't carry over may be present
no comparison arm with opt-out or active choice
relevance_reason: A short-term, liquid savings product (unlike pensions) that directly measures opt-in take-up and 12-month retention, the outcome pairing the brief most wants evidence on.

key_finding: Characterizes optimal default-option design analytically, showing that when the designer and choosers agree on an activity's value, some form of weighted opt-out minimization is asymptotically optimal, with extensions for externalities, Pigouvian fees, and normative disagreement.
methodology: Theoretical/mathematical modeling of optimal default design with numerical simulations to validate asymptotic approximations. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Offers a general normative frame for when minimizing opt-out (i.e., defaulting people in) is actually optimal versus not, relevant background for justifying (or not) an opt-out default, but it is abstract theory without empirical grounding in our setting.
limitations: Purely theoretical, no empirical application to consumer savings or fintech
no discussion of engagement, withdrawal, or perceived manipulation
relevance_reason: General economic theory of optimal defaults that could frame the decision abstractly, but too disconnected from consumer-app specifics to directly move the design.

key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing that EU regulation of choice architecture is fundamentally about protecting consumer autonomy rather than banning influence per se.
methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis constructing a normative taxonomy from EU statutes and case law. Abstract-only.
why_it_matters: Gives the legal test for whether pre-selecting round-up enrollment or a pre-set multiplier reads as a helpful default versus a regulable autonomy violation — directly bears on which of the three entry designs Legal's clearance actually survives reputational and regulatory scrutiny for.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not empirical evidence on enrollment or amounts
general consumer law, not financial-product specific
relevance_reason: Only shortlisted paper addressing the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the entry decision.

key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs. roughly half opting out at lower historical defaults), and low-income employees were disproportionately likely to remain stuck at a suboptimal default.
methodology: Administrative panel data from a single employer plan with a high default contribution rate; includes a literature review of opt-out rates at lower defaults.
why_it_matters: Shows that raising a pre-set level does not proportionally raise opt-out, and that low-income users anchor hardest on unfavorable defaults — a caution against blindly pre-selecting the highest multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
single employer, no direct amount-saved comparison beyond 12 months
relevance_reason: Directly informs the anchoring-on-preset-level question via a very high default contribution rate, though in the excluded employer-plan setting.

key_finding: Abstract text is corrupted/missing ('Trant'), so no findings can be extracted beyond the title's implication of UK payroll savings automation experiments.
methodology: abstract-only; abstract content unavailable to assess design or scale.
why_it_matters: Title suggests short-term (liquid) payroll savings experiments, which would be closer to the round-up product's liquidity profile than retirement studies, but nothing can be confirmed from the available text.
limitations: abstract is essentially empty/corrupted
cannot verify sample, effect sizes, or methodology
likely payroll-linked rather than fully self-directed consumer setting
relevance_reason: Shortlisted for topical fit (automating short-term savings) but abstract provides no usable evidence.

key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, but consumers still capture less than half of the potential savings available from cheaper liquidity sources.
methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments across major UK banks.
why_it_matters: A directly analogous consumer-banking-app automatic-enrollment intervention with real effect sizes and evidence that even a well-targeted default leaves substantial value unrealized — useful benchmark for what to expect from opt-out round-up enrollment.
limitations: alerts, not a savings/contribution feature
does not report multi-month enrollment persistence or opt-out rates specifically
relevance_reason: Closest available analog: automatic enrollment in a UK consumer banking app with quantified financial outcomes and heterogeneity in who benefits.

key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised average savings by £32-38/month but also raised unsecured debt by £7/month and mortgage balances by £118, showing that headline savings gains from a default are partially offset by increased borrowing.
methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from randomized roll-out of UK automatic enrollment pensions across ~160,000 small employers, with 41-month administrative follow-up.
why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help' premise: enrollment gains can be partly illusory once offsetting debt behavior is accounted for, which is exactly the support team's disengagement/vanity-metric worry applied to net financial position rather than just withdrawal.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a liquid consumer savings app
debt offset mechanism may not apply to small, liquid round-up sums
relevance_reason: Best available long-horizon evidence that automatic enrollment's savings effect is confounded by behavioral offsets, directly relevant to whether defaults change real net saving.

key_finding: Adding a minor enrollment 'ordeal' (extra step) to health insurance auto-enrollment reduced enrollment by 33% and disproportionately excluded young, healthy, and economically disadvantaged people, undermining the standard efficiency rationale for ordeals in adverse-selection markets.
methodology: Natural experiment studying removal/addition of an auto-enrollment ordeal step in a public health insurance program, with a supporting selection model.
why_it_matters: Strong distributional warning: friction added to enrollment (analogous to opt-in vs. opt-out or active-choice friction) does not screen neutrally — it disproportionately drops disadvantaged users, a direct caution for the entry-design decision's equity concerns.
limitations: health insurance selection market, not a financial savings product
no data on amount saved or persistence, only enrollment
relevance_reason: Directly on point for who is helped/hurt by enrollment friction, a core brief question, despite being in a different consumer-choice domain.

key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 of tax-subsidy expenditure raised total saving by only 1 cent because only ~15% of 'active savers' respond (mostly by shifting existing assets), while automatic (passive-default) employer contributions raised wealth substantially among the 85% of 'passive savers.'
methodology: Large administrative panel analysis of the full Danish population's savings responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive default contributions.
why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that active-choice mechanisms mostly reshuffle assets among the financially sophisticated while passive defaults are what move genuinely new saving — a central data point for weighing active choice against opt-out.
limitations: retirement account setting with tax subsidies, not a liquid consumer round-up feature
pre-dates the app/fintech and EU dark-pattern regulatory context
relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative distinction between active and passive savers that the brief's active-choice question directly engages with, though outside the consumer app setting.

key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice with loss-framing that favors one option — as a way to get most of the automatic-enrollment benefit without a full default, explicitly recommended as a complement to or substitute for opt-out enrollment.
methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing standard active choice, enhanced (framed) active choice, and opt-out defaults on behavior-change outcomes.
why_it_matters: Supplies a concrete third design — not plain active choice but a framed variant — that the round-up feature's onboarding screen could adopt to capture more of the opt-out enrollment lift while avoiding forced-default disengagement; the specific technique (loss-framed active choice) is explicitly proposed as a savings-context substitute for automatic enrollment.
limitations: primary domain is medication adherence, not financial products
abstract gives no quantified effect size for enhanced active choice itself
relevance_reason: The one paper offering a specific, transferable active-choice design technique rather than just comparing active choice to opt-out in the abstract.

key_finding: A broad review of household finance covering savings, borrowing, payments, and interventions (education, defaults, product design, choice architecture) that firms and governments use to shape financial behavior, without giving a single pooled effect size.
methodology: Narrative literature review/book chapter synthesizing empirical regularities and intervention research in household finance.
why_it_matters: Provides the broader taxonomy of choice-architecture levers (defaults, product design, disclosure) into which the entry and level decisions fit, useful context for framing the design space even without a specific effect estimate.
limitations: synthesis, not a systematic review with pooled effect sizes
spans both employer and consumer contexts without disentangling them
relevance_reason: Only broad synthesis in the shortlist covering choice architecture and product design in household finance generally.

key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment lifted participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half remained at the default rate even after three years.
methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms before and after automatic enrollment adoption, tracked over several years.
why_it_matters: The canonical demonstration that a pre-set level anchors the chosen contribution rate for years, not just at signup — the strongest direct precedent for worrying that a pre-selected round-up multiplier will become 'sticky' regardless of what users would otherwise choose.
limitations: employer 401(k) setting, foundational/older study predating app-based fintech
no data on withdrawal or disengagement, only contribution-rate persistence
relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-on-default-level result the brief's C3 question is built around, despite being outside the consumer-app setting.

key_finding: Randomized default enrollment into a salary-linked savings account raised participation by 40 percentage points (equivalent to a 50% match), driven mainly by present bias and the cognitive cost of evaluating savings scenarios, and also increased subsequent active saving after the study ended.
methodology: Randomized field experiment among employees in Afghanistan with follow-on interventions isolating mechanisms behind the default effect.
why_it_matters: Offers a mechanistic account (present bias, cognitive cost) for why defaults work, which helps predict whether the round-up default will merely capture inertia or actually build a saving habit that persists post-default.
limitations: salary-linked account in a very different economic/regulatory context, not an EU consumer banking app
short-term liquid round-up savings differ from the account studied
relevance_reason: Provides causal mechanism evidence for the default effect that generalizes better than pension studies, useful for predicting persistence.

key_finding: A field experiment on a Brazilian financial-management platform found payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, with users who already overdraft seeing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer fintech/financial-management platform.
why_it_matters: Direct evidence, in a self-directed consumer fintech app, that a well-intentioned automated nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the heterogeneity risk the brief warns against building blind to.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or savings contribution levels
Brazilian credit-card market, not EU round-up savings
relevance_reason: Best available consumer-fintech evidence of distributional harm from automated interventions, directly answering the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' question.
